Business Justification and Return on Investment: ROI, Payback Period, Total Cost of Ownership

Unit 1: Financial Management. Lesson 5 of 60 in CHTM Academy.

A vendor contract on your imaging system renews in four months at $180,000 a year. You believe two trained technicians and a parts budget could do most of that work for less. Nobody will take your word for it. What gets funded is a business justification with the numbers inside it, and what gets rejected is the same idea described in a hallway.

The business justification document

Written in one order and never another.

  1. The problem, in the hospital's terms: cost, downtime, risk, or a regulatory exposure, with the number attached.
  2. The options, including doing nothing, each described well enough to be chosen.
  3. The costs of each option across the same number of years.
  4. The benefits, separated into dollars you can defend and benefits you cannot price.
  5. The risks of the option you are recommending, and how each is handled.
  6. The recommendation, one option, stated plainly, with what happens if nothing is funded.

Return on investment, worked

ROI = (gain minus cost) / cost x 100. Take the real case: a $25,000 training program and tool package that lets your staff absorb work you now buy, avoiding $90,000 of contract cost in the first year.

Gain avoided                              $90,000
Cost of the investment                    $25,000
Gain minus cost                           $65,000
Divide by cost            65,000 / 25,000       2.6
Times 100                                   260%

An ROI of 260 percent says each dollar invested returned itself and $1.60 besides, inside the year. Positive is the pass mark; what gets funded is the highest return among competing requests.

Payback period, worked

Payback = cost / annual savings, in years. A $100,000 project that saves $20,000 a year pays back in five years. Shorter is better, and finance usually has an unwritten ceiling, so ask what it is before you write the memo. Payback and ROI answer different questions: ROI asks how much the investment returns, payback asks how long the hospital's money is at risk.

Total cost of ownership

TCO is every dollar a device costs from purchase to disposal: purchase price plus installation and site preparation, service and parts across the life, training, software and licensing, consumables, and disposal. Compare TCO, never sticker price. A system that is $40,000 cheaper to buy and $25,000 a year more expensive to maintain loses on a ten-year TCO by a margin no purchase discount recovers. State the number of years in the comparison, because an unstated horizon is how a bad option wins.

Soft benefits, stated so they count

Uptime, patient safety, faster response, clinician satisfaction, and staff retention are real and resist pricing. Do not hide them and do not inflate them. State each as a measurable change with a baseline: response time on this equipment type falls from the current measured figure, repeat repairs fall, satisfaction scores on the departments served rise, with the dates you will report them. A soft benefit with a measurement attached survives the meeting. One stated as "better service" does not.

Exam tip: ROI = (gain minus cost) / cost x 100, payback = cost / annual savings, and TCO is the whole life, not the purchase. The justification runs problem, options, costs, benefits, risks, recommendation, and always says what happens if nothing is funded.
Remember
A funded request is a written justification that runs problem, options, costs, benefits, risks, and recommendation, with ROI as gain minus cost over cost times 100, payback as cost over annual savings, and total cost of ownership rather than the sticker price.
Deeper explanation

Business Justification and Return on Investment: ROI, Payback Period, Total Cost of Ownership, explained slowly

The first case: insourcing a contract

The imaging service contract renews at $180,000 a year. You propose training two technicians and stocking parts instead.

INVESTMENT (year one)
Service school, two technicians, tuition                      28,000
Travel and lodging                                             9,000
Test equipment and tools                                      22,000
Initial parts inventory                                        26,000
Total investment                                              85,000

ANNUAL EFFECT (from year one)
Contract cost avoided                                       180,000
New annual parts and consumables                             (34,000)
Retained vendor support for the one module staff cannot
  service                                                    (22,000)
Net annual saving                                            124,000
ROI, year one       (gain - cost) / cost x 100
                    (124,000 - 85,000) / 85,000 x 100            45.9%
Payback             cost / annual savings
                    85,000 / 124,000                         0.69 years,
                                                             about 8 months
ROI, cumulative     (124,000 x 2 - 85,000) / 85,000 x 100       191.8%
through year two

Read both numbers. The first-year ROI of 45.9 percent is positive but unremarkable, because the investment and the saving both land in year one. The payback of about eight months is the number that wins the meeting, because it says the hospital's money is at risk for less than a fiscal year. State which year an ROI refers to, every time, or the figure means nothing.

The second case: a project with a long payback

The same department proposes a $240,000 test and calibration facility that lets the hospital stop sending test equipment out and start calibrating for two nearby clinics.

INVESTMENT
Build-out, bench, and environmental control                  165,000
Reference standards and calibration equipment                 61,000
Training and accreditation preparation                        14,000
Total investment                                             240,000

ANNUAL EFFECT
Outside calibration cost avoided                              31,000
Revenue from the two clinics                                  18,000
Added consumables, reference recalibration, and
  record keeping                                             (11,000)
Net annual benefit                                            38,000
ROI, year one       (38,000 - 240,000) / 240,000 x 100           -84.2%
Payback             240,000 / 38,000                        6.3 years
Five-year position  (38,000 x 5 - 240,000) / 240,000 x 100       -20.8%
Ten-year position   (38,000 x 10 - 240,000) / 240,000 x 100       58.3%

This is a real proposal and a bad one at most hospitals, and the arithmetic is what tells you so. A payback of 6.3 years will fail almost any finance ceiling, and the investment does not turn positive until year seven. Bringing this to a committee without the ten-year line is dishonest; bringing it with the ten-year line and no acknowledgment of the ceiling is naive. The useful version of this proposal is smaller: buy the reference standards, keep sending the hard items out, and revisit.

Total cost of ownership, compared properly

                                 System A        System B
Purchase price                    410,000         370,000
Installation and site prep         26,000          48,000
Service, 10 years                 180,000         310,000
Parts outside contract, 10 years   40,000          62,000
Training                           14,000          22,000
Software licensing, 10 years       30,000          55,000
Consumables, 10 years              88,000          88,000
Disposal                            4,000           4,000
Ten-year total cost of ownership  792,000         959,000

System B is $40,000 cheaper to buy and $167,000 more expensive to own. State the horizon, state every line, and let the committee see that the discount on the sticker was the smallest number on the page.

Soft benefits with measurements attached

Soft benefit        How to state it so it counts
Uptime              availability on these devices, from the current measured
                    figure to a target, reported monthly
Response time       total time to repair on this equipment type, baseline to
                    target, from CMMS data
Safety              use error and repeat repair counts on the fleet, baseline
                    to target
Satisfaction        the department's survey score for technical competence and
                    responsiveness, unchanged instrument, same question
Retention           voluntary turnover in the shop, with the replacement cost
                    avoided named

What to memorize

ROI               (gain - cost) / cost x 100; say which year
Payback           cost / annual savings, in years; shorter is better
TCO               purchase + installation + service + parts + training +
                  software + consumables + disposal, over a stated horizon
Justification     problem, options, costs, benefits, risks, recommendation
Always include    what happens if nothing is funded
